A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renaming and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original centralized and federated classification experiments, efficiency measurements, and appendix studies of distillation and polynomial approximation.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original SBS results, baseline comparisons, feature-similarity analyses and FHE measurements.

M1.justification: V2 adds stochastic block sampling (SBS): nonadjacent block representations are selected, and unselected features are zeroed for adapter learning. Appendix B.1 additionally introduces noise masking of unselected outputs during client decryption and re-encryption. These substantially extend the privacy procedure; polynomial approximation, distillation, parallel adapters and secure aggregation are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Fed-ISIC2019 for downstream classification, with Tiny-ImageNet and Fed-ISIC2019 auxiliary data. The additional component, similarity and cost analyses do not expand the represented datasets, domains or downstream tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 1–4 add evaluated LoRA and adapter-tuning comparators throughout the accuracy, scalability and efficiency comparisons. Appendix D.1 identifies federated LoRA as FedIT. Full fine-tuning and linear probing remain; the additions go beyond their existing citations in v1.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation procedures for adjacent versus nonadjacent block similarity using eight-sample batches, and a separate per-block FHE benchmark at 128-bit security with single-sample and batch-of-eight measurements. These substantially broaden evaluation beyond classification and approximation testing. The retained classification experiments keep their splits, optimizers, learning rates, training budgets and balanced-accuracy metric.

E4.justification: V2 adds BlindFed-versus-BlindFed+SBS comparisons, feature-similarity heatmaps examining permutation vulnerability, and comparisons of block-sampling strategies in Appendix B. Appendix D.5 adds encryption-overhead analysis. V1's auxiliary-data, client-scalability, distillation and approximation-degree studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or empirical error bars. The added SBS sampling probabilities concern the algorithm's behavior, not uncertainty estimates for reported performance.

E6.justification: Existing accuracy entries in Tables 1–3 are unchanged under the Ours-to-BlindFed rename, but substantial LoRA, adapter-tuning and SBS results are added. For example, the new SBS row reports 0.6831 on federated Fed-ISIC2019 with in-distribution auxiliary data, versus retained BlindFed accuracy of 0.6679. Table 7 newly reports 136 seconds for encrypted block inference and 17.33 MB ciphertexts. Table 4 changes Fed-ISIC2019 memory from 17.32 to 8.71 GB for linear probing and from 8.71 to 17.32 GB for full fine-tuning.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a sampling-probability recurrence, its stationary probability of one-third, and approximate expected sampled-block counts. Proposition 1 and its non-uniqueness proof are retained and relocated to Appendix A; the distillation and approximation mathematics remains substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: V2 makes SBS a core contribution and explicitly focuses the introduction on cross-silo adaptation. The abstract shifts from preventing extraction through permutation to mitigating extraction through permutation and SBS, while qualifying feasibility with substantial communication and server costs. The conclusion changes from describing the challenges as addressed to stating that practical adoption still requires important improvements.

C2.justification: V2 acknowledges that neighboring representations can undermine permutation-only protection and motivates SBS through that mechanism. It interprets SBS's mixed accuracy effects as limited disruption and possible regularization, extends the existing communication caveat with a large-model/small-data applicability argument, and identifies rigorous model-privacy guarantees and malicious-client robustness as unresolved.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link, descriptions of the evaluated baseline implementations, and substantial FHE implementation information: Tile Tensors/CKKS, 128-bit security, representation dimensions, and the benchmark machine and RAM. These are new disclosures; the PDFs do not establish a change to the implementation or hardware of the retained classification experiments.

R1.justification: V2 adds LoRA-GA, LoFT, linear-probing and FHE implementation/acceleration references while retaining the existing research positioning. The additional published FedIT reference corresponds to federated instruction-tuning work already cited in v1, rather than a distinct new work.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion, names the framework BlindFed, and reorganizes the method around architecture redesign, two-stage split learning and privacy boosting. The proof moves to the supplement, existing appendix material is reorganized, and a contents page is added. This restructuring extends beyond the newly added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds an overall workflow diagram, an SBS state diagram, similarity heatmaps, sampling plots and an FHE-cost table, and redraws existing architecture illustrations. Tables 1–4 gain comparator rows and double-blind-status columns. V1's accuracy-versus-parameters plot is removed, new efficiency bar charts are added, and retained training curves are regrouped with clarified loss-axis labels.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central feasibility and privacy claims through relevant PEFT comparisons, analysis of permutation vulnerability, measured FHE costs and a more qualified conclusion. These address important evidentiary gaps in v1. End-to-end model privacy remains unestablished, and the claimed SBS communication savings conflict with Appendix B.1's continued transmission of masked blocks. Nevertheless, the expanded evidence and clearer deployment limitations provide a substantial net quality improvement.
